node.label: Margaret MacMillan
node.date_label: Women of the Raj (1988) · Peacemakers (2001) · The Uses and Abuses of History (2008) · The War That Ended Peace (2013)
node.description: In Peacemakers (2001; published in the United States as Paris 1919 in 2002), Margaret MacMillan argues that the peace negotiators have been blamed too readily for later failures, restoring attention to their choices and constraints. The Uses and Abuses of History (2008; US title Dangerous Games, 2009) examines how claims about the past serve present identities and political purposes. Her international history balances individual decisions with wider social, economic and ideological pressures. Women of the Raj (1988) studies British women in colonial India, while The War That Ended Peace (2013) asks how peace gave way to war. Christopher Prior praises the latter’s clarity but questions whether its narrative gives sufficient weight to the forces favouring peace. War: How Conflict Shaped Us (2020) broadens the inquiry to warfare and social organisation; Walter Scheidel criticises its accumulation of anecdotes and its failure to distinguish wartime invention from the acceleration of changes that might otherwise have occurred.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Women of the Raj (1988); Peacemakers (2001), US title Paris 1919 (2002); The Uses and Abuses of History (2008), US title Dangerous Games (2009); The War That Ended Peace (2013); History’s People (2015); War: How Conflict Shaped Us (2020).
node.scope_note: Selected primary excerpts from Dangerous Games and War, complete autobiographical essay, selected interview answers and named reviews read. proposed_edges.relationship: In Learning the Scholar’s Craft (2021), MacMillan acknowledges Tuchman’s influence; note 1 identifies The Zimmermann Telegram (1958) and The Proud Tower (1966).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Essay paragraph beginning Yet all the time: “a huge influence”; note 1 names both works. Neither Tuchman book read here; no specific doctrine or exclusive influence asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: In War: How Conflict Shaped Us (2020), MacMillan quotes Tilly’s formula that war made the state and the state made war, according to Anthony Wilson-Smith’s review.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Wilson-Smith’s review reports a quotation of Tilly; it does not establish adoption of Tilly’s wider account. The publisher preview consulted here does not contain the Tilly passage. Retain counts_toward_floor=false.
proposed_edges.map_label: Reported quotation of Tilly on war and the state

proposed_edges.relationship: Reviewing Canada and NATO: Uneasy Past, Uncertain Future (1990), jointly edited by MacMillan and David S. Sorenson, Granatstein recommends the collection while finding some essays overtaken by events.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete CBRA Review section and Contributor header: “a very good book”, qualified by intervening events. This is reception of a jointly edited volume, not praise of every MacMillan argument; the reviewer singles out Halstead, English and Bercuson. Book body unread; review date unspecified.

proposed_edges.relationship: Women of the Raj (1988) contributed a study of British women in colonial India to the expanding field of women’s history, as MacMillan explains in Learning the Scholar’s Craft (2021).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Essay paragraph beginning Because Ryerson, with note 4: “women’s history” and the decision to write about British women in India. First-person field positioning; no claim about Indian women’s perspectives or a full gender theory. Monograph unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Peacemakers (2001; US title Paris 1919, 2002) reconsiders diplomatic responsibility for the postwar settlement and contests treating the negotiators as scapegoats for subsequent failures.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Hachette description, final paragraph: “unfairly been made scapegoats”; Oxford research statement, final paragraph, balances individuals and wider forces. Publisher-mediated account of the argument; full book unread. Original and reissue years separated.

proposed_edges.relationship: The Uses and Abuses of History (2008; US title Dangerous Games, 2009) examines how remembered pasts help construct identities and sustain political claims.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Leonard interview, answer to Why is this so fraught: “history is a very important part of identity”. Publisher excerpt, The History Craze, paragraphs on heritage and collective attachments. Remembered identity is distinguished from the public-institution edge below; complete book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In The Uses and Abuses of History (2008; Dangerous Games, 2009), MacMillan examines how museums, heritage policy and popular media shape public encounters with the past.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, chapter 1, from Museums and art galleries through the heritage-policy examples: “Governments tend to assume”. Specific sites of public interpretation, rather than institutional membership or influence on every public historian. Displayed excerpt read; remaining book unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: In The Uses and Abuses of History (2008; Dangerous Games, 2009), MacMillan disputes the claim that experiencing an event gives someone superior historical understanding.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Leonard interview, questions/answers from Being there through the Cuban Missile Crisis discussion: eyewitnesses “only know a small part of the picture”. She calls for wider evidence. This is a limited epistemological intervention, not an argument against using testimony; book read only in separate excerpt.

proposed_edges.relationship: War: How Conflict Shaped Us (2020) argues that war and human society are so deeply intertwined that the capacity to make war and the evolution of society are part of the same story.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary publisher PDF preview, introduction pp. 1–5: “War is not an aberration” (p. 2); reciprocal war/society argument pp. 4–5. Selected first-chapter publisher excerpt also read. Full book unread. Scheidel’s named criticism remains in entry prose; no community knowledge reproduced.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her review essay “Von Hötzendorff’s Desire” (2004), MacMillan challenges Ferguson’s suggestion that Britain might have been wiser to stay out of the First World War, questioning the consequences of a quick German victory in light of German expansionism and occupation practices.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The complete publisher-hosted 2004 review of David Stevenson’s Cataclysm was read. The paragraph naming Ferguson asks what a quick German victory would have entailed, then discusses the character of imperial Germany and German atrocities, exploitation and destruction in occupied Belgium and France. This is direct engagement with a named argument, not an inference from shared subject matter. The review does not identify a Ferguson book title; no particular Ferguson monograph is attributed or claimed read. The critic points toward the position criticized.
proposed_edges.map_label: Challenges the case for British non-intervention

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2016 review of History’s People: Personalities and the Past (2015), Joanna Bourke endorses MacMillan’s argument for individual choices and actions in historical explanation, interpreting its counterfactual questions as devices for understanding what actually happened.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Full review read in the 21 March 2016 capture of the magazine’s own page. Bourke distinguishes her general dislike of counterfactual history from her favourable assessment of this book. This records substantive review reception, without inferring intellectual debt. The original book’s 2015 publication is checked separately with House of Anansi; the review discusses the British edition. Joanna Bourke is an existing person endpoint.

proposed_edges.relationship: History’s People: Personalities and the Past (2015) contributes to biography and life writing by using the lives of historical actors and observers to examine individual agency and the recording of everyday experience, as the Publishers Weekly review explains.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Complete review read on the review journal’s own site. It discusses the book’s structure and its treatment of diarists, rather than merely listing subjects. House of Anansi separately dates the original publication to 2015 and explicitly identifies the relationship between biography and history as the book’s subject. The book itself was not read; no wider influence on biographers is asserted.

proposed_edges.relationship: Women of the Raj (1988) contributed an early account of British women’s gender disadvantage under empire; Indrani Sen’s Gendered Transactions (2017) places it in a phase that portrayed the memsahib as a victim of a male-dominated colonial enterprise, before later scholarship more fully examined women’s simultaneous colonial privileges.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s introduction, especially pp. 1–3 and note 2. The sample is linked directly from Manchester University Press’s book page. Sen identifies MacMillan’s place in the historiography and qualifies the earlier victim-centred approach against later gender-and-empire studies. This edge retains that limitation and does not credit MacMillan with those later analyses. It adds the gender-history endpoint; the input’s separate women’s-history pair is retained without duplication. Sen is absent from the allowed person endpoints, so no Sen–MacMillan edge is proposed.
